title: No Distractions
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens sesshin by reading a poem by Rosemerry Wahtola Trommer about forgetting to build the wall between us, then takes up Dongshan's answer when a monk asks what Yunyan meant by "just this is it." Nomon recalls sitting with a dying stepmother and asks whether sesshin aims at complete stillness. A ten-part list of states, from contact and expansion to distraction, numbness, and intention, serves as a map, and each state gets the phrase "just this is it." One example is a Tassajara neighbor who wrote plays in his head during a retreat. Nomon closes by asking the room to hold the question "What's my intention?" without an answer.

sentences.text: *One morning, we will wake up and forget to build that wall we've been building, the one between us.
The one we've been building for years, perhaps out of some sense of right and boundary, perhaps out of habit.
One morning we will wake up and let our empty hands hang empty at our sides.
Perhaps they will rise as empty things sometimes do when blown by the wind.
Perhaps they will simply not remember how to grasp, how to rage.
We will wake up that morning and we will have misplaced all our theories about why and how and who did what to whom.
We will have mislaid all our timelines of when and plans of what, and we will not scramble to write the plans and theories anew.*
*And that morning, not much else will have changed.
Whatever is blooming will still be in bloom.
Whatever is wilting will wilt.
There will be fields to plow and trains to load and chickens, sorry, children to feed and work to do.
We chickens too.
And in every moment, in every action, we will feel the urge to say thank you.
We will follow the urge to bow.
One morning we will wake up and forget to build the wall we've been building, that one between us.*
*The one we've been building for years, perhaps out of some sense of right and boundary, perhaps out of habit.
One morning we will wake up and let our empty hands hang empty at our sides.
Perhaps they will rise as empty things sometimes do when blown by the wind.
Perhaps they will simply not remember how to grasp, how to rage.
We will wake up that morning and have misplaced all our theories about why and how and who did what to whom.
We will have mislaid our timelines of when and plans of what.
And we will not scramble to write the plans and theories anew.
On that morning not much else will have changed.*
*Whatever is blooming will still be in bloom, whatever is wilting will wilt.
There will be fields to plow and trains to load and children to feed and work to do.
And in every moment, in every action, we will feel the urge to say thank you.
We will follow the urge to bow.*
Isn't that nice?
This is a poem somebody sent me.
I don't know much about the poet.
Her name is Rosemary Watola Traumer.
Maybe later on we'll find out who she is and how she could write a perfect sesshin poem for us.
I'm so grateful to get to be together again, for each of us for being here.
And what a remarkable beginning, this many people, all of us attending so carefully to the quiet, to coming, to following the schedule.
It's amazing.
You put these things out there, and no matter how many years this theory gets disproved, I think there always is and always will be a part of you that thinks nobody's going to come.
And then you have the big orientation and there's great excitement, and then you get up at five next morning like nobody's going to be in there.
So you're a wonderful bunch of nobody.
Thank you.
Somehow.
And I want to especially thank my colleagues who worked so hard to put this together.
There's lots of scrambling, as there often is, maybe more than usual in the last few weeks, to get everything just right.
So I want to thank Talus and Kate McKenna, who couldn't be here, and Chris and many, many other people.

And how wonderful it is just to stop and just to be, just to breathe, to step out of that busy frame, to put down trying too hard, like she says in the poem, to let our hands just rest, to drop it all.
We can't explain why this is so valuable and what's wrong with doing stuff.
Somehow it seems to be so essential to our human development to have a time of not doing.
But we still got to try to explain this all, and so we can't help ourselves.
Six talks this week by myself, Michael and Norman, who, as I mentioned, is arriving tomorrow afternoon.
And as we mentioned, he's right now at Stanford, and probably this very moment actually.
I don't remember the exact schedule, but I think the talk he's giving is this morning at Stanford Memorial Church, which they call Memchu.
I grew up hearing about Memchu.
So maybe he's also giving a talk about doing nothing to the brilliant young people graduating from Stanford.
That would be a good thing.
Maybe encouraging them also to connect with the peacefulness of just being a person, just built in, that we don't have to fix or figure out.
But maybe we have to shut up and sit down long enough to remember that we are of that nature.
And of course, it's a bit of a conceit to say we're not doing anything.
We're always doing something, even in sesshin.
So what does it mean to be doing or not doing?
We really don't stop doing until we die.
I was recently with a loved one who died, and one of the things I noticed is there's great effort and hard work right until the final moment.
It's the effort to breathe.
The body's engagement with aliveness is so beautiful and so powerful.
And then it lets go.
And then there's really stopping.
And unbelievably peaceful to sit in the room with her for a few minutes.
I say sitting with her, but do we know if her body is still her?
Where do we go?
I just feel so grateful to have had that in that moment, that teaching from my stepmother.
And maybe it's essential training for us to learn what it is to be a human being that can do and not do.
Maybe it's really important to learn that we all at some point are present at the beginning and at the end, at a birth and at a death.
Of course we will inevitably all be present at least at one birth and death.
But maybe it will help us to make the best use of the time in between if we also support others in their moments of being born and their moments of dying.
Probably we won't have this experience this week, as far as we know.
Nobody is that pregnant in the room, and we hope nobody is that close to death.
But maybe we will, who knows.
But also we'll see many births and many deaths in our own experience.
Sometimes it's really overwhelming how many things are being born and dying inside our heart, inside our mind, all the time.
Some of the things being born we like.
I think we're out of batteries.
Maybe, I don't know.
We checked it.
Is it okay if I speak like this, or should we make an effort with the PA?
It's okay.
Okay, I'll really try to project.
And if you're in the back, if you just hold up your hand, I'll know that that's what you mean.
So sometimes an overwhelming amount of things are born in our heart, in our mind.
Some we like, some we don't like.
Many things die.
Some we are happy to see be rid of.
Even living this simply for a week, our experience is so full, don't you think?
So rich.
And there's a part of us that really would like complete peace from all of this.
A part of us that maybe would like to actually stop in that full way that only can happen at death.
We hunger, I think, for some more peacefulness.
For slowing down a little more.
Maybe we look pretty still from the outside.
But I think we all know by now, the secret is out.
It's not just you.
We're not always so peaceful on the inside.
So is the goal of our sesshin to be completely peaceful?
Completely still?
Completely stable?
Is sesshin a tool or technique to make that happen?
Or help that happen?
Is somehow the craziness of our mind also sesshin?
We really don't know what to do with our mind and how to practice.
Even if we've been doing this for a long time, we really don't know.
So we can look a little bit to our ancestors, see what they had to say.
That's one of the wonderful things about our tradition.
We have these little stories and little leavings, little hints and sayings from the Zen ancestors, given in a context just like this.
So here's one of them, as a way of expressing maybe what we're trying to do.
*As Dongshan was presenting offerings before the image of his teacher Yunyan, he retold a story from before about depicting reality.
A monk came forward and said, when Yunyan said, just this is it, what did he mean?
Dongshan said, at that time I nearly misunderstood my late teacher's meaning.*
*The monk said, did Yunyan himself know it or not?
Dongshan said, if he didn't know it, how could he be able to say this?
If he did know it, how could he be willing to say this?*
Let me read that again with a few clarifying notes about what the scene is.
Dongshan's the teacher in this scene and we're reflecting on his teacher named Yunyan, and there's also a student there who doesn't get a name.
He's just the monk, or she's just the monk.

*Dongshan was presenting offerings, making offerings at the altar before the image of his teacher Yunyan, and he retold a story from before about depicting reality,* presumably how his teacher helped him to understand reality.
*The monk came forward and said, when Yunyan said, just this is it, what did he mean?* So we're to understand this is a phrase that Yunyan taught to Dongshan.
Just this is it.
So Dongshan's student is saying, well, what did he mean?
*Dongshan said, at that time I nearly misunderstood his meaning.
At that time I nearly misunderstood my late teacher's meaning.
The monk said, did Yunyan himself know it or not?
Dongshan said, if he didn't know it, how could he be able to say this?
If he did know it, how could he be willing to say this?*
So many of these turn on this question: is there anything to say or not?
To each other, to ourself.
Whenever we're saying something, we need to have a relationship with experience.
All these sayings are about that in some way, it seems.
What is our relationship to experience?
I've always loved Yunyan and many stories about him and his Dharma brother Dao Wu.
So look them up.
Yunyan was the teacher of Dongshan, who's also very famous in this group of teachers who we idolize as important in our lineage.
It's our literary conceit that there's this group of like 30 men, sorry, they're all men, who created this world of practice.
We know of course they were constellated around a much bigger reality, and there were of course many women there, and there was another thousand years after that too.
So some other stuff happened, probably.
But still it's wonderful to take them up as poetical figures and as ancestors with that inclusive frame.
So Dongshan somehow brought up regularly, he must have, Yunyan's teaching phrase, just this is it.
And you have to love Dongshan's humility in the story.
When his students ask about that, the first thing he says is not some explanation but: I didn't get it either.
I nearly didn't.
It's hard to understand.
And somehow his student can see a feeling underneath that statement of humility, and he asks, well, did your teacher himself know it?
Did he understand it?
How did he understand it?
Something like that.
So is there anything to understand here?
Is there something to get?
Is Dongshan teaching some wisdom that's a something that we will get, that will help us when we understand it, if we practiced carefully enough or long enough or hard enough?
What is it we can actually know?
And of course that's how we think, right?
We want something, or maybe we want to be rid of something, which is the same thing.
Dongshan's bringing up a couple of facets.
That there's a kind of knowing, but maybe it's a knowing without a separate kind of knowledge.
A knowing without knowledge may be a way.
When he talks about Yunyan's understanding, saying if he didn't know it, how could he say it?
There's something there.
But if he did know it, why would he be willing to say it?
He would know that anything he would say, you know it, you know you don't know it.
But we have to say something.
We have to do something as long as we're alive.
We do seem to need some way to work with this mind and heart.
And our main method this week looks like it's zazen.
Seated meditation.
And of course we're doing lots of other things, even our simple life, if you think about it.
We're all in one way together.
But I think zazen appears most frequently on the schedule, so it must be the main thing.
So what is our goal in zazen?
What is it we hope for?
The word for this ritualized week is sesshin.
As far as I can make out, sesshin is composed of two characters, Setsu and Shin.
This is an odd Japanese concoction.
Maybe it's a little bit like church Latin: different ways of pronouncing Chinese characters depending on the context.
So this is not like modern Japanese.
Setsu, the first character, seems to mean to touch or make contact with.
And Shin means heart or mind or heart and mind.

So the title suggests that in order to figure out the great knowledge or calm down or get better, it just says we're here to touch our heart, to touch our mind, to contact our heart and mind in some way.
And of course all kinds of experiences arise in sesshin, but somehow as we settle [unclear: "and instantly use any verb"] what if I don't settle?
Should I give my money back, get out of here?
So somehow, as whatever it is happens, there does seem to be some kind of contact in some way.
Of course how it shows up is different for every person, as different as every mind is.
Which makes total sense.
Even though we look more or less the same, we have the same number of limbs and eyes, all of us are fortunate, and we all recognize each other as human beings.
Thanks to the guidelines, we're all dressed more or less the same too.
So we look more or less the same, but of course we know we're very different.

Each of us is at the head of our own karmic trajectory, pushed along into this room by our past, our habits, our tendencies, the collection of thoughts, the emotions that we string together, more or less coherent, something that we call myself, my personality, my psychology.
So each of these very different me's is meeting this contact with heart and mind a different way, of course.
When I started practicing, I noticed there was a kind of ban on talking about your meditation experience.
It was kind of verboten.
The idea, as far as I can remember, I don't know if they even said what the idea was.
Maybe what I made up about the idea.
And I noticed that about Zen: it's very prone to all this making up of different reasons for why things are.
You go to the various teacher meetings and say, "Oh, this is because of this."
"Oh no, no, no."
So who knows why, but there was a ban in those days, in that place anyway, on talking about your meditation experience.
And maybe the idea was we just confuse each other.
Our experiences are so different.
Maybe somebody might describe an experience that sounds really great, really desirable to you, and who knows what that would trigger.
Or maybe the opposite: someone would describe just being a complete wreck, terrible, awful experiences, and you feel better, you make a little progress.
So it makes sense.
Maybe it's better to say nothing, certainly simpler.

I think it was also implied that the wise Zen masters could and should be told about your meditation experience, because they know all about meditation experience and would receive it with complete equanimity.
And I think we hold both of these views a little more lightly now.
It's okay to talk a little bit about meditation experience, and maybe the wise Zen teachers don't know all about it either.
I feel like we can trust each other to have at least a little equanimity, goodness.
Our varied meditation experience isn't really a secret.
We all know that all kinds of things are happening for us in all kinds of ways all the time.
But maybe it isn't that interesting to talk about it too much.
I remember Norman used to say you should get more interested in your own mind, because it's helpful to share, helpful to say out loud to others, and to explore in our own minds in a clearer way.
And it can also be profoundly helpful in releasing some of our projections on each other on the path, to hear a little about the foibles of each other's minds in meditation.
It can be pretty funny too.
And interestingly, now when I teach the secular practice, it's actually the opposite practice.

We deliberately talk regularly about meditation experience as a practice, a practice of speaking about experience as experience, to start to notice, through the doing of this, the many ways we go quickly to judgment, summary, projection, deep memory.
It's pretty fun.
I hope you get an opportunity to do this with people, without all this heavy spiritual path thing going on.
Just sit a few minutes and say, "Well, what did you notice about your own mind?"
And almost inevitably, the first time you do this with a group of people, so notice if you do this to yourself now, you do a little meditation, yes, and what do you notice?
Almost every single time the first person to speak starts to notice.
Sometimes, if they're lucky and you're lucky, you can suggest, "So I heard those words.
Is that a description of experience?"
"Oh, it's a judgment."
Yes.
So quick, right?
And we identify with our judgments so strongly.
So in sesshin we are not, of course, talking to each other about our meditation experience or anything, but that does not mean we are not listening a little to our own mind.
We recognize we are talking to ourselves 24/7, always talking, talking, talking to ourselves in some way.
So how do we talk to ourselves about our experience?
How do we approach this desire for settling, for contact with something?
How do we work with loving that feeling, that we may feel, of expansiveness and openness and settledness and really seeing the beautiful sunset at nine o'clock tonight?
You know, there's going to be a beautiful sunset, but will you notice?
So we want something, we want something from our experience.
So what do we do when we're not getting that, when it's not happening, when we feel overwhelmed instead, when we feel resistant, just hurt, when we're really stuck in something?
So does Yunyan's phrase "just this is it" apply in some way here?
Just this is it.
Is that true when our experience feels like the opposite of meditation?
Just this.
No.
I want to share with you a list I received from one of my teachers.
I don't know exactly where she got it.
I'll find out later.
It seems like a helpful list, and I'm going to share it even not totally knowing its provenance.
In this list there are ten categories of experience.
So it's like a scheme, like a model, many models in Buddhism, and of course we're always constructing different models in our minds of what our experience is, of who we are.
Sometimes we don't notice that we're in one of these ten categories.
So just contemplate whether this might be helpful, to be curious about whether we're in one or more of these ten categories in any given moment.
The first category is called contact.
We already talked a little bit about this.

It's what we want, most of us most of the time: contact with the moment, in place, contact with each other, contact with peacefulness and connection, just really being present as a kind of contact, in a way touching in.
We have lots of different phrases for this: being grounded, contact with the ground, being balanced, kind of contact with the balance point.
So that's the first category.
The second category is expansion, and this was presented originally.
It was like a big wheel, like contact leading to expansion.
Who knows if it really goes around in a big wheel.
But wheel models always feel appropriate to sesshin, right, because it always feels a little bit like you're spinning around and around and around.
So the second in this model is expansion, the heart opening, springing out of contact, perhaps that narrow feeling of me and my agenda just dropping away, opening up.
Sometimes expansive meditation experiences can be so joyful, if ultimately a little confusing, because we get excited about them.
That's another story.
So: a sense of expansion, a sense of opening up, very pleasant.
And of course you might feel that contact and expansion are the goal, and whatever the rest of the list is, it's got to be some other stuff.
But then we wonder: can we really exclude a whole swath of our experience as non-meditation, or non-sesshin, or non-me, or non-human?
Let's consider some other options.
And I have to talk about them in a fairly dramatic way to make the point, but of course these things show up much more subtly too, and interwoven.
So the third category is overwhelm.
Maybe that openness leads too much into floods of emotion, difficult memories, worry, pain.
You know, "What was that thing about it being peaceful here?
It's horrible."
Overwhelm, really challenging.
Of course we try to let it go.
Maybe we try to return to the breath in the belly.
Maybe we try not to add more anxiety and worry to our overwhelm.
Of course we're going to seek relief, but sometimes there is no relief to be had.
Overwhelm is overwhelmed.
So the question here is maybe we can be with overwhelm as part of the path.
Maybe our self-talk can be, not just "How do I get out of this?" but "This is overwhelmed.
I can just be with this."
Maybe Yunyan's phrase, and pop in with the breath: just this is it.
Overwhelmed.
For the rest of the world.
Overwhelmed.
The fourth state in this model is distraction.
The mind just won't settle.
Famous monkey mind.
We hardly even know where we are or what's happening.
The bell rings.
We're like, "What?"
We're surprised.
Maybe a little ashamed.
Another good Zazen period wasted.
Sometimes distraction has an enticing, creative quality to it.
None of these are necessarily a bad thing or a good thing.
Not good or bad.
I was pleasantly distracted by a nice little bit from a song in Zazen recently.
Maybe you were too.
I remember one of my neighbors at Tassajara Zendo telling me he'd written some wonderful plays in his mind during a long retreat.
And you couldn't remember them later, but they were great plays.
You know, like big awards.
I don't know if that was part of the fantasy too.
Other times distraction is not so coherent.
It's just noise, kind of random.
"Where did that come from?"
That's the other thing in talking about experience with novice meditators.
That's a common thing too: "Where did all this come from?"
So distraction, distraction, distraction.
Just this is it.
So can we just be with distraction?
And that's what's happening.
The fifth state is unconscious, or unconsciousness.
We go to sleep.
We check out.
Our body is still here but we're gone.
This can include vague states we can't quite put a name on, kind of woozy states, maybe some sense in the mind of almost remembering something, or just plain nodding off.
People often come to the dokusan room seeking relief from this.
"How do I stop nodding off?
It's horrible."
And we always try to come up with something to help them, but I don't know if anything really helps besides just being with sleepiness, just being with unconsciousness as long as it has you.
An essay I like to read sometimes about permission in meditation, By giving ourselves permission, has a line like, *you have permission to go to sleep in meditation.
How else will you ever learn about waking up?* Isn't that good?
Maybe there's something to be learned from sleepiness.
Maybe we can snooze a little bit with Yunyan's phrase.
Just this is it.
The sixth and the seventh of the ten states are avoidance and rejection.
I had to list them together because they go together so well.
We want out of here.
We are totally justified in wanting out of here, because the food is wrong, the cabins are too funky.
Norman's pretty good, but I don't know about these other jokers.
Where is Norman anyway?
I have so much to do.
What am I doing wasting my time here?
I don't have time for this.
So can we recognize this as avoidance and rejection?
You may be curious about it.
What is it we're really actually trying to avoid?
What are we rejecting?
And even here, to be able to know our avoidance and know our rejection as part of the path.
Just this is it.
The eighth and ninth meditation states, or general states, you know, this is like all day, these go together too: feeling fake and going numb.
Feeling fake and going numb.
So it's the flip side of avoidance and rejection in a way.
The main problem is not the external world, according to our mind.
The problem is not sesshin, the problem is me.
I'm not doing it right.
I'll never learn how to do it right.
Make the same mistakes every time.
I'm basically faking it and they're going to find out sooner or later.
And the more symbolic stuff you get on, [unclear: "my educator, my neighbor"], whoever, I'll never be as good as her.
And maybe a strategy for dealing with all of this feeling of being a fake is going numb.
It doesn't really matter.
Who cares?
I like the talks okay, so I'll just sit here all day and suffer until the next one.
Probably leave, but it's embarrassing to leave.
So, you know, we all have this, right?
And so interesting to see if we can bring awareness to even this, even numbness, even feeling of fake.
And of course, all these things get totally mixed together.
No one thing ever appears by itself, right?
We know that.
We're distracted.
We don't get up right away when the han sounds.
I'll be late anyway.
My body hurts.
I think I'll stay in my room.
And of course, it's pleasant for me to get a laugh, so I do that.
But we can notice these things much more subtly, moment by moment, swirling and changing.
In one moment, a feeling of contact, a little expansiveness, a little overwhelm, right, to distraction, checking out, coming back, feeling a little numb or a little numb.
They all weave together.
So we can just be curious about these, if they feel helpful to you as a kind of map or compass for exploring our own experience.
Not so that we can cleverly avoid all these undesirable states, but so that we can know our experience as it is.
And then the last one might be the whole system.
The tenth state is intention: noticing our intention, noticing when our attention is present, maybe to some extent nurturing our intention.
This is seen as very powerful in Buddhism, a quality of mind that can turn the wheel right around.
And we can play with different kinds of intention for a while, see how that works.

Another intention might be in alignment with this teaching from Yunyan and Dengxuan: intention to let it all in and be present with it, to honor all states as equally human, equally real and equally unreal, just what is, to nurture the intention with lots of patience.
So in the last few moments of the talk, let's just check in with our own intention.
If you need to rearrange yourself so you're a little more comfortable, let's find a stable place.
If you're kind of in that, I'm just going to say, perhaps, the openness of your heart: what's my intention?
What's my intention in coming here, being here?
If you don't know, that's okay.
It might be the best way to practice with intention, just to ask that question without an answer.
What's my intention?
Ask yourself again.
Thank you for that.
Anything that happens is practice, is path.
If we don't like something and want to exclude it from our sesshin, we can feel what that does, and maybe we'll catch ourselves in the act of doing so.
Maybe we'll see each state as each state.
Maybe we can breathe with just this is it.
Another model, you know, will come to mind to support you in playing with your relationship to experience.
Probably we can't fix our experience.
Maybe there's some freedom in our relationship with it.
Distractions as meditation, not as the enemy of meditation.
Thank you again very much.
